limitations: Focused check-evasion sample. Strata select cases and do not assign the reference. Single engine-assisted reviewer used ordinary root and played replies before seeing the candidate outputs.

cases.rationale: Nf6+ exchanges the knight with tempo before the queen and rooks can reorganize. The two quieter queen choices allow damaging checks or a queen exchange. The g3 passer shapes all routes.
The rook and queen attack the king in the two higher-rated capture lines. The played Rxg2+ allows Kxg2 and yields a substantially weaker attack with a different defence.
Rxd1+ is competitive and demands a particular answer to the check. Exchanging rooks buys queen activity, while the other leading moves keep the rook active on the d-file.
Qh7+ and Qc2+ keep the queen active against the king and control the advancing b-pawn. Kg2 is the reliable defence in the competitive checking line.
Rg6+ displaces the king before the rooks invade the second rank. Rxc4 or Re6 allows a rook exchange or a different defensive formation without the same invasion.
Nxg3+ gives Black a forcing recovery after Rxg3, while the queen checks alone let White retain the better-coordinated attack.
The two leading moves require calculation against the bishop checks and the pawn on g2. The worse queen move fails to answer the threat on d7.
Rf3+ displaces the king and supports the d-pawn promotion sequence. The alternative king or knight move changes how the passer is covered.
Rd3+ restricts the king and enables the passed pawn advance through more checks. Pushing c3 immediately is also viable. Kf5 allows White to liquidate the passer.
Rxe1+ forces a king move before taking the other bishop on b1. Capturing on b1 first or moving the king lets White preserve more counterplay.
Black needs a concrete answer to threats against the uncastled king and bishop. Rc8 applies pressure to c4, while Qf4+ still allows the queen's invasion.
Ne2+ creates the knight entry to c3 with tempo. Nb6 or b5 instead allows White heavy-piece tactics on the b-file.
Rg8+ restrains the king before Ra8 defends the a-pawn from behind. The other moves let Black take the passer and hold much more easily.
Rh3+ coordinates the bishop and rook against the opposing rook and pawn structure. The comparably rated bishop moves have different continuations and no specific short tactic is established.
The rook check, king improvement and a-pawn push reach comparable lines. White's targets are g6 and the weak queenside squares.
Bxf2+ wins the rook with check and keeps the bishop. Rxf2 instead allows Bd6 and a concrete exchange sequence, with a much smaller advantage.
Qf7+ forces the queen exchange and gives the rook access to the seventh rank. Delaying it allows Black to take on a4 and defend differently.
The black king supports the central passers. Ra2+, Ra5 and Ra7 give similar positions through king activity and rook control.
Qxf5+ exchanges queens with tempo and reorganizes the bishop and rooks. Rg5 permits Qxe6+ and loses the exchange by force.
Rd8+ and Bd5+ force the knight exchange before the rook takes on d5. The quiet rook or bishop moves give Black more freedom to reorganize.
